https://www.azernews.az/region/264078.ht.text: Hungary plans to end Russian gas imports by October 2027 18 September 2026 14:21 (UTC+04:00) Ulviyya Poladova Read more Hungarian Minister of Economy and Energy Istvan Kapitany said that Budapest expects to ensure its gas supplies without Russian gas by October 2027. In an interview with Telex, Kapitany noted that the government was holding active talks with neighboring countries, including Romania, as well as companies supplying liquefied natural gas (LNG), as Budapest looks for alternatives to pipeline gas from Russia. Asked whether Hungary would be able to halt Russian pipeline gas imports by October 2027, in line with the European Union’s requirements, Kapitany pointed to existing cross-border infrastructure and alternative supply routes. "Thanks to the infrastructure of the import routes and the availability of different sources, Hungary’s gas supply will be secured next October," Kapitany emphasized. The minister also added that if developments proceed as currently expected, Hungary’s gas demand could be met through alternative sources, although he cautioned that the situation remains difficult to predict. Kapitany is serving as Hungary’s economy and energy minister in Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s government, which was formed in May 2026. Earlier Magyar insisted that the country would seek compensation from Brussels for abandoning Russian energy resources. The comments come as Hungary examines ways to diversify its energy supplies and reduce dependence on Russian energy. Photograph: Tim Ockenden/PA Immigration and asylum Planned asylum seeker detention centre next to Oxfordshire sewage works criticised Thames Water says detainees at proposed accommodation should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells Camille Corcoran and Rajeev Syal Sun 15 Nov 2026 11.47 EST First published on Sun 15 Nov 2026 01.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Home Office plan to build asylum seeker detention facilities next to a sewage pump is facing objections after water company officials warned that detainees should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells. Proposed secure accommodation blocks at Campsfield House immigration removal centre in Oxfordshire will be 20 metres from a sewage pumping station, according to a written submission from Thames Water. A senior development manager at the company wrote that it could give rise to “amenity effects, including odour, noise, vibration, lighting associated with maintenance activities, insects and flies” for any inhabitants. In a previous submission, the company wrote that any development may lead to sewage flooding. The warnings, which come as the government hopes to expand the immigration detention estate by 40%, have been seized upon by campaigners against the expansion. Ally Swadling, the lead legal education officer at the charity Right to Remain, said: “Thames Water’s concerns about sewage infrastructure at Campsfield show how little regard is being given to even the most basic standards of sanitation and human dignity. “They reinforce what we already know – this government is putting its political priorities above people’s lives and wellbeing.” The centre near Kidlington re-opened in December 2025 after it was shut in 2018 following years of problems, including suicides, riots, escapes and complaints about conditions. The Home Office is planning to increase the centre’s capacity from 160 bed spaces to 400, and to convert existing buildings. According to the Thames Water submission in October, officials also “raised concerns regarding capacity within the foul water, surface water and water supply networks” in the local area. A separate 2015 written consultation response , which was submitted in June, states the development may lead to sewage flooding in the area. “Thames Water request that an impact study be undertaken to ascertain, with a greater degree of certainty, whether the proposed development will lead to overloading of existing infrastructure,” it said. Written representations, including that of Thames Water, will be heard at a public inquiry beginning on 14 December. Oxfordshire county council has formally objected to the expansion of Campsfield House, saying it risks intensifying existing public concern, and called for the site to be shut permanently. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Average of 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News UK Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox after newsletter promotion According to the Home Office, nearly 80,000 people have been returned or deported from the UK since the 2024 election to the end of June 2026, an increase of 52% on the previous two years. Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said: “Detention is a harmful, dehumanising experience that must only be used as a last resort. Evidence shows it’s ineffective, expensive and damages people forced to endure it. “Instead of expanding sites such as Campsfield House immigration removal centre, and in this case, in a way that could potentially be detrimental to the health and wellbeing of people staying there, the government must instead use community-based alternatives detention, which have proven to be effective and much cheaper.” A spokesperson for the Home Office said: “We are confident in our plans for Campsfield immigration removal centre and will continue to engage constructively with the Planning Inspectorate as the process moves forward. We are committed to increasing the removal of those with no right to remain in the UK. Expanding our detention capacity plays an important role in achieving this.” Thames Water said they had nothing to add to their response. https://www.express.co.uk/travel/europe/.text: Home Travel Europe This market needs to be on your list (Image: Getty) November is here, and that means that across the UK and Europe , Christmas markets are beginning to set up. Although in the UK it’s a bit of a coin toss as to whether there will be snow at Christmas, there is one place where you are most likely to have a white Christmas . Although it’s not in the UK, it’s less than three hours from London. Plus, this gorgeous market has consistently been named one of the best in Europe - and it's home to the oldest public Christmas Tree. Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, is the home of one of the best Christmas markets in Europe and the most likely to see snow. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT The Express visits Manchester's Christmas markets According to research from Rome2Rio , the market has averaged 28.1 days of snow over the last 19 Christmases. The market runs from November 20 to January 6, and it fills the medieval Town Hall Square with festive charm. Liverpool Echo lifestyle reporter Christopher Megrath visited this gorgeous market and said it was among the most beautiful he had ever seen. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT He wrote: “The Old Town Christmas market in Tallinn, Estonia, was by far the most beautiful I’ve ever experienced. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “Unlike its famous Christmas market rivals in cities like Vienna, Cologne, or Salzburg, Tallinn’s market is modest in size. I had never heard it mentioned in conversations about Christmas markets, nor did I know anyone who had even visited the country, yet what it lacks in international fame it more than makes up for with its enchanting setting, cosy atmosphere and magical charm.” 8 beautiful Christmas markets where you can still get flights under £100pp 'World's most liveable city' is a European gem with great life expectany The Tallinn Christmas market is one of the best (Image: Getty) You’ll be spoiled for choice at this market which offers everything from handcrafted trinkets, chocolates, Christmas decorations and hand-knitted scarves and gloves to keep you cosy in the freezing December weather. RTE ranked the Tallinn market as the best in Europe, and highly recommended that tourists try out the ice-skating rink and the old-fashioned carousel. You can also try sipping on some hot spiced wine made from local buckthorn berries and spiked with liquor for an especially indulgent Christmas tipple. The market will open at the end of November, and stays open from 10am to 8pm with hot drinks served all the way through to 10pm.
